items.body: Idaho nonprofit Envision helps provide eye exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. (Photo by Getty Images) Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision , figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss. Jay Lugo is the executive director of Envision, an Idaho 501(c)(3) nonprofit that receives hundreds of inquires a month about help with vision care and eye exams. (Photo courtesy of Envision) Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way. “I’ve seen people break down and cry when they put on a pair of glasses and discover they are able to see,” Lugo says. “It fills my heart with joy being able to do that – and I sleep well at night knowing that we are making a difference. But it’s not just me. It’s the volunteers and office co-workers who see that happen, and the 1,400 Lions Club members throughout the state who get information about what’s being done. So, a lot of people are involved.” And Lance Grady of Boise is glad for that. He didn’t break down in tears when he recently was fitted with glasses, but he did look across a street and see a squirrel climbing a tree. And he could see letters, numbers and names on buildings. “I wouldn’t have been able to see any of that without my glasses,” he said. “This has been life changing. I can drive and do other things that I was unable to do.” Grady’s story began by word of mouth. “A family friend talked with me about reaching out to the Lions,” he said. “They were determined to help me find something – without spending $400 for a pair of glasses. “I’m so thankful … a lot of stress has been lifted from me.” Lugo has seen similar stories play out many times. “When people are able to see, they can get a driver’s license, fill out a job application and be productive,” Lugo says. “There is such a big gap with healthcare, and we’re only talking about eyesight and hearing. The state doesn’t provide aid with eyeglasses for those over the age of 18, so you are not going to get eyecare assistance if you are at the poverty level.” Envision helps fill the void, providing exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. Envision offers free vision clinics for those at, or below, the poverty levels, and Lugo says demand is high. “I get at least 20 applications in my email box every day, which is about 600 a month,” he says. “Every one of those are from people who need glasses and are at the poverty level. There are a lot of people who are hurting.” Envision started in 1969 as Idaho’s only eye bank and arranging corneal transplants remain a big part of the nonprofit’s operation – along with the tradition of collecting and refurbishing used eyeglasses. People throughout the state can drop off glasses at the Division of Motor Vehicles, Walmart opticals and local optometry offices. “It’s important to note that November is National Donate Eye Month,” Lugo says. “As I’ve seen first-hand, Idaho is a giving state with the nation’s largest registry per capita. Idaho is at 62 percent, and the national average is around 38 percent.” Envision has opened a retail operation that is available to people throughout Idaho. “This gives us a sustainable source of revenue, beyond grants,” he said. “People still will get glasses at a free or discounted rate, but we’ll be able to provide something else. All people need to do is download a prescription and we can ship directly to those living in Idaho, or the United States.” Donations – large and small — will continue to be crucial to Envision’s success. items.summary: House Speaker Mike Moyle, standing at right, speaks to the 2026 Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state legislator pay will be frozen in place at $25,000 for the next year, in line with state employees who did not get a pay increase from legislators this year. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Then, starting Dec. 1,
items.body: House Speaker Mike Moyle, standing at right, speaks to the 2026 Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state legislator pay will be frozen in place at $25,000 for the next year, in line with state employees who did not get a pay increase from legislators this year. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Then, starting Dec. 1, 2027, the annual base pay for legislators is set to increase by about 6.7%, up to $26,685. Members of the 2026 Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation voted 5-1 to approve holding legislative pay flat for one year and then increasing it next year. House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, had recommended increasing the base pay to $26,685 starting Dec. 1 of this year, but the committee held pay flat this year after committee members Tom Harris and Bryan Mooney pointed out that state employee pay was held flat this year. “I have that in the back of my mind for the citizens and other state employees that didn’t get a raise, and I think it sends the right message if they didn’t get a raise,” Mooney said Thursday. In addition to the base pay, an unstructured constituent services allowance all legislators receive will increase to a flat $6,000. Most legislators previously received $2,500 per year in constituent services allowance, although legislators who live in geographically large legislative districts received up to $5,300. Moving forward, there will be no distinction between district sizes. Under the Idaho Constitution, state legislators do not have the power to set their own pay. Instead, the six-member Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation is responsible for setting legislator pay and benefits. The committee is made up of three appointees from the governor and three appointees from the Idaho Supreme Court. None of the committee members may hold a public office that is compensated with pay, according to the Idaho Constitution. The Idaho Legislature is not in session, but will be soon. The 2027 legislative session begins Jan. 11 at the Idaho State Capitol. Before that, the Idaho Legislature will convene for the organizational session in early December. Idaho legislators pay is set to go up, while state employees have gone without a raise Since 2024, the pay raises given to state legislators have been significantly larger than the raises for regular state employees, which are set by the Idaho Legislature. In 2024, the last time state legislators received a pay increase, the Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation approved a 25% increase in legislative pay, from $19,913 a year to $25,000 per year. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US Meanwhile, state employees have not received any pay increase since 2025 as the Idaho Legislature prioritized cutting state budgets and expenses during the 2026 legislative session to pay for costs of conforming to the tax changes in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The last time state employees received a pay increase in 2025, legislators approved raises ranging from $1.05 per hour to $1.55 per hour, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. The percentage of pay increase was different for each employee depending on their salary, but for many state employees the pay increase was less than 3%. In 2024, legislators signed off on raises of up to 3% for state employees. Many state legislators have careers, businesses and incomes outside of their legislative service. But for Idaho’s more than 20,000 state employees, their job and their pay is their livelihood. Moyle, the speaker of the Idaho House, told the Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation that state legislators will increase pay for state employees next year. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. Hospitals leaders who got awards say they'll make a big difference. Some smaller facilities who didn't get any funds say navigating the program was difficult without dedicated staff. (Getty Images) After Idaho health officials had to “sprint” to award all of its nearly $186 million federal rural health care grants, a number of small health providers say they were left without answers about why their applications were denied. Juliet Charron was named director of the Department of Health and Welfare in September 2025. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare) Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron met with state legislators on the Rural Health Transformation Committee and healthcare providers and stakeholders on the Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force in two separate meetings on Thursday in Boise. The Rural Health Transformation Program was created through the $50 billion Congress approved in July 2025 through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which also reduced an estimated nearly $1 trillion over 10 years in Medicaid spending nationwide. Idaho received about $186 million in the first year, and federal authorities announced on Nov. 9 the Gem State would receive nearly $183 million in year two. Charron said staff are trying to determine why the state received less in the second year. More than $103.5 million of Idaho’s grants in the first year were awarded to hospitals and clinics for infrastructure projects, equipment and technology upgrades in rural hospitals. “The (electronic health record software), this is transformative for us. This is something that for us to do on our own, would take almost all our cash on reserves,” said Brad Turpen, CEO, Valor Health. Valor Health, in Emmett, received two awards, totaling more than $5.4 million for a new electronic health record system that will connect to larger hospitals in the area, and new imaging equipment. John Hennessy, CEO, Bonner General, said his hospital will be able to expand its surgical capacity by adding four new suites. The 25-bed hospital is the only hospital in the county, he said, and its operating room was at full capacity. “A lot of our patients either have to wait long extended periods of time to get their surgeries done, or they end up traveling outside the area to get those procedures,” he said. He said the volume of surgeries is expected to increase 23% in the first year with the new space that will be added. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.summary: The debate over expanding (or killing) Idaho’s private school tax credit entered a new stage Friday — when the Idaho State Tax Commission released a damning and detailed trove of data on the $50 million program. items.body: The debate over expanding (or killing) Idaho’s private school tax credit entered a new stage Friday — when the Idaho State Tax Commission released a damning and detailed trove of data on the $50 million program. The commission report handed a lot of ammunition to opponents of the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit. The critics probably don’t have the political juice to repeal the program. However, they have some new and hard numbers on their side. The tax credits largely benefitted wealthier families. The average adjusted gross income for tax credit recipients came in at $178,000. The credits largely benefitted families who were already outside the public school system. Only 25% of the tax credits supported students who had ever attended a public school — suggesting that a lot of money went to parents who were already homeschooling their children, or sending their kids to private school. The credits largely benefitted families in urban and suburban Idaho. The Tax Commission ranked applications by legislative district (and remember, legislative districts are drawn up to have more or less the same populations). Six of the top 10 districts are in Ada or Canyon counties; two more take in pieces of Kootenai County. These three data points are crucial. They tie straight into the debate over the tax credits — which became law in 2025, with the passage of House Bill 93 . Supporters said the $5,000 to $7,500 credits would open education options to families who could not otherwise afford to leave the public school system. The credits, they said, were about providing access and supporting choice. When the Tax Commission data came out Friday — and supporters and opponents alike went straight into the spin cycle — the advocates latched onto numbers supporting their version of the narrative. They pointed to Tax Commission numbers from May : About 45% of tax credit recipients had household incomes at or below 300% of the federal poverty level (now $99,000 a year for a family of four ). In a kind of glass-quarter-full argument, the pro-tax credit Mountain States Policy Center said Friday, “3,092 awarded students — 25.3% — had previously attended public school.” Mountain States also pointed out that the tax credits made their way into households in each of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. “The data is even more surprising given that opponents claimed there were no choice options available in rural areas,” wrote Chris Cargill, Mountain States’ president, in a Sunday post defending the tax credit and criticizing news coverage of the Tax Commission’s data drop. This is all factually accurate. Some lower-income families took advantage of the credit. Some used the money to move their children out of public schools. Some explored learning options in rural communities with limited private school options. Any of the above. All of the above. However, statistics don’t just show the exceptions to the rule. They also lay out the contours of the rule itself. So, yes, residents of legislative District 34, Madison County, collected a little more than $200,000 in tax credits. But at the same time, residents in District 20, in and around Meridian, collected close to $3.6 million. Madison County is the exception. Meridian is the rule, along with similar urban and suburban districts. The Tax Commission presented a statistical aggregate. The prototypical tax credit recipients live in a six-figure household, most likely reside in or near a population center, and quite possibly they had their kids in private school long before House Bill 93 came along. That’s the prototype. And it’s an inconvenient one for supporters of the program. Which leads us to the 2027 legislative session. Saying the Tax Commission’s numbers illustrate a “rousing success,” Mountain States pounded away at expansion last week . items.summary: The entrance to the hearing room for the Idaho Senate's State Affairs, Resources and Environment, and Education committees as seen on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) After months of waiting, last week the Idaho State Tax Commission finally released information about which parents are receiving the $50 million in voucher
items.body: The entrance to the hearing room for the Idaho Senate's State Affairs, Resources and Environment, and Education committees as seen on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) After months of waiting, last week the Idaho State Tax Commission finally released information about which parents are receiving the $50 million in voucher money. Idaho parents who got new private tax credit earned average of $178,000 per year, report shows Surprise, surprise, the Tax Commission report says most of the money is going to families that earn more than double the income of the average Idahoan and students who have never attended public schools. The average family that received voucher money this year earned $178,000, more than double the $84,234 of the average Idaho family. This makes the voucher program a government handout for families who can already afford to send their kids to private schools. Moreover, 75 percent of the families who took the money have never had their kids enrolled in a public school, even though advocates for the program promised that it would help students leave so-called “failing public schools” to attend private ones. And of the 25 percent of families whose kids did attend a public school, only 4.6 percent were enrolled for an entire school year a year ago. Critics of the voucher program warned that it would mainly benefit families living in urban areas rather than in rural communities. As expected, two thirds of the voucher money went to families living in just three counties – Ada, Canyon, and Kootenai. Furthermore, nearly 25 percent of the money went to only five private schools, most of them religious schools: Bishop Kelly High School in Boise, Cole Valley Christian in Meridian, Nampa Christian School, The Ambrose School in Meridian and Logos Classical Christian School in Moscow, which is led by Christian Nationalist Doug Wilson. Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, D-Boise, speaks during a Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 13, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, a retired teacher, was one of the leading opponents of the voucher program and on Friday reacted to the Tax Commission report: “It’s hard enough for working parents to make ends meet without being asked to subsidize private school tuition for families who are better off than they are.” Ward-Engelking said someone should “explain to a rural parent why their child’s school can’t afford another teacher, but the state can afford to help a well-off family pay private school tuition. That’s a pretty lousy deal for rural Idaho.” Nothing in this report should be a surprise to Gov. Brad Little or the legislators who voted to create the voucher program. They were warned that voucher programs across the country benefit the rich, and families that never sent their kids to public schools, and urban families over rural families. Still, Republican legislators, most of them rural, voted for vouchers and Gov. Little signed it into law, even though 32,000 Idahoans contacted his office and asked him to veto the bill. Vouchers, which are unpopular among most citizens, was one of the major issues in the country during the recent mid-term election. The issue contributed to the election of Democratic governors and legislators in many Republican states which adopted vouchers. In Texas, longtime Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, the leading advocate for school vouchers in the Lone Star State, lost to a Democrat who made her reputation by opposing vouchers while serving in the Legislature. items.summary: Idaho can tap into several existing revenue sources — and a few new sources — to compete in a changing college athletics landscape. That’s the takeaway from a gubernatorial working group, which spent the summer and fall looking at Idaho college athletics. Its work product, an eight-page report , went public Wednesday. “Do we want to compete on the national stage? If the answer is yes, no single pr
items.body: Idaho can tap into several existing revenue sources — and a few new sources — to compete in a changing college athletics landscape. That’s the takeaway from a gubernatorial working group, which spent the summer and fall looking at Idaho college athletics. Its work product, an eight-page report , went public Wednesday. “Do we want to compete on the national stage? If the answer is yes, no single proposal in this report will be enough,” group chair Cortney Liddiard, an Idaho Falls businessman, wrote in the report. “Idaho needs Idaho solutions, pursued together.” The report outlined the group’s proposals — albeit in general terms: Three existing funding sources could boost athletic coffers: interest earned on tuition and fee payments; withdrawals from the Higher Education Stabilization Fund, a state budget reserve; and a streamlined process for approving capital projects in athletics. Four new revenue streams also could be on the table: state lottery proceeds; a “transaction fee” on sports prediction markets; revenue streams from existing, university-owned properties; and state and local legislation to allow athletic programs “to benefit from the economic activity they generate.” The report affixes no dollar figures to any of these revenue sources. And the available money could vary widely. For example, state lottery proceeds are already spoken for; this year’s record $90 million payouts went to public schools and building projects. The stabilization fund, meanwhile, is a standalone fund dedicated solely to colleges and universities, with about $25.6 million in hand. While Wednesday’s report was short on specifics, it conveyed a sense of urgency. A battery of court cases could reshape the college sports landscape. Meanwhile, Congress is considering a far-reaching bill that would reshape college athletics; it has passed the Senate but is stalled in the House. “For these reasons, Idaho’s approach must remain flexible,” the report said. Closer to home, the State Board of Education has given Boise State University the go-ahead to cover an athletics shortfall of up to $18 million — with much of the deficit spending going to “revenue sharing” payments to Boise State athletes. “That was a prudent bridge, but it is not a practice that can or should be repeated,” Liddiard wrote. “Absent meaningful action, the board will have little choice but to require the department to eliminate that deficit, with consequences that would profoundly diminish Boise State’s ability to compete.” In a news release Wednesday, Boise State President David Hahn commended the working group. “We are carefully reviewing the report and look forward to working with the governor, Legislature, State Board and our fellow institutions to identify a path forward that strengthens college athletics across Idaho.” On Wednesday, Gov. Brad Little called the report a strong starting point. “College athletics matter to Idaho,” Little said in a news release. “They bring our communities together, carry our state’s name across the country, and help attract the students and talent our economy needs.”

items.body: When Alan Pesky’s son Lee was in the fourth grade, Alan was called in to see the headmaster. Lee was, supposedly, underperforming and acting out. The headmaster recommended that Lee would fare better in a different school. Alan got the message: “That was shorthand for he’s not very smart. The words at that time, back in the early 70s, were that the child is dumb,” he said. But Alan knew Lee was not dumb. “On the contrary — he was curious and intelligent; he just didn’t fit neatly into the picture of the school’s typical student,” Alan wrote in his memoir, “More to Life than More.” It was eventually determined that Lee had learning disabilities, but in the 70s and 80s, the diagnosis was fairly new. Alan and his wife, Wendy, struggled with finding their son the correct resources to help him. “When Lee was a child, the words “learning disability” weren’t even in the English language,” Alan said. “We didn’t have knowledge at that time of what special education and learning disabilities were all about.” Alan struggled to understand his son for many years. He said he had a hard time grasping Lee’s disabilities, which led to friction in their relationship. Sadly, in 1995, when Lee was 30, he died from a cancerous brain tumor. The loss profoundly changed Alan, and to honor his son, he was devoted to advancing research and resources for other kids like Lee. In 1997, Alan and Wendy founded the Lee Pesky Learning Center (LPLC) in Boise. “[My dad] and my mom started the Lee Pesky Center at probably the toughest times in both their lives,” said Greg Pesky, Alan and Wendy’s youngest son. “They had this crazy idea of how we could memorialize Lee … and they came up with the Pesky Center.” What started as a place for kids with dyslexia to receive tutoring has turned into a holistic approach to understanding and aiding students, families and teachers with special education resources. The programming has served at least 100,000 students and 7,000 teachers in every Idaho county over the years. Now, less than a month away from 93, Alan travels across the country, splitting his time between New York and Idaho. Although he is retired, he is still deeply involved with Lee Pesky Learning Center. “In fact, yesterday I was on a meeting for two hours with the Lee Pesky Learning Center,” Alan said. “What happens with the Lee Pesky Learning Center, and the impact that this organization can still have in the future is something that continues to excite me at my ripe old age of 93.” Alan reflects on how a place like the Lee Pesky Learning Center could have helped his family. “It would have made an enormous difference in Lee’s life,” Alan said. Despite Lee’s hardships, he graduated from Lafayette College in Pennsylvania in 1987 and became an entrepreneur. Lee co-founded The Buckin’ Bagel, a Bagel shop with multiple locations in the Boise area in the ‘90s. “If Lee were here, I would put my arms around him, give him a hug and say to him, I may have been a little difficult during your early years, but I have so much pride in how much you have achieved,” Alan said. Former Timberline students sue over expulsions related to online comments
items.summary: Former students at Boise’s Timberline High School have filed a federal lawsuit, saying they were unfairly expelled amidst a public outcry over threatening online comments. The comments on the Snapchat social media platform — a graphic thread that discussed raping and killing a female student — were “crude and distasteful,” the former Timberline football players’ attorneys acknowledge in the lawsui
items.body: Former students at Boise’s Timberline High School have filed a federal lawsuit, saying they were unfairly expelled amidst a public outcry over threatening online comments. The comments on the Snapchat social media platform — a graphic thread that discussed raping and killing a female student — were “crude and distasteful,” the former Timberline football players’ attorneys acknowledge in the lawsuit. But the thread was not “a serious expression of an intent to commit violence,” according to the lawsuit. Meanwhile, the attorneys said, district leaders had already publicly condemned the online comments, promising to bring the students to justice. “Plaintiffs were denied a meaningful opportunity to present their defenses to the allegations before the decision was made to punish them,” according to the lawsuit, filed Nov. 6 in U.S. District Court in Boise. The lawsuit came barely a month after the content of the social media thread went public — prompting an Oct. 3 online petition calling for immediate disciplinary action and an Oct. 7 student walkout at Timberline. Before the walkout, district officials canceled or postponed Homecoming activities at Timberline, saying the firestorm over the online thread posed a threat to safety. The lawsuit says district and school officials quickly suspended the four players involved in the “Gameday lunch” Snapchat thread. The suspensions stretched for 17 days, and according to the lawsuit, the players were not given a chance to be heard. Near the end of the 17-day suspensions, according to the lawsuit, Timberline Principal Chad Wright recommended removing the students from school, assigning them to Boise Alternative to Suspension and Expulsion school or Boise Online School for fall semester, or the remainder of the year. Three of the four students are assigned to online school for the semester or the school year, and a fourth is under a tutoring plan. The district held hearings before permanently removing the students from Timberline, the lawsuit said, but the students were not given adequate time to prepare a defense. Ultimately, the students were reassigned not because of their online comments but because of “the public’s reaction to those communications and the disruption it caused,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit does not identify the students by name — only as John Does Nos. 1 through 4. One plaintiff, identified only as Jane Roe, is the legal guardian of John Doe No. 4. The lawsuit names five Boise school administrators as defendants: Superintendent Wendy Johnson; Deputy Superintendent Nick Smith; Shelley Bonds, the area director for Timberline and neighboring schools; Jason Hutchinson, the Borah area director who oversaw the students’ disciplinary hearings; and Wright. District spokesman Dan Hollar declined comment on the lawsuit Tuesday. A criminal investigation is ongoing. “(The Boise Police Department) has reviewed the evidence currently available and will continue to evaluate additional evidence as it is received from the social media platforms,” spokeswoman Haley Kramer said in an email Tuesday. “It is anticipated that it will take time to receive and evaluate this additional evidence and interview additional witnesses based on that new information.” More reading : Click here for coverage from the Idaho Statesman, which first reported on the lawsuit.

items.body: A cryptocurrency kiosk, right, at a Royal Farms gas station in Wallops Island, Va., stands ready to accept cash for a variety of crypto products including Bitcoin, Dogecoin and Ethereum. The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. (Photo by Barb Barrett/Stateline) States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines continue to mount, costing Americans nearly $389 million last year alone. Four states — Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont — enacted statewide bans this year, while dozens of communities have moved to prohibit the machines or impose new restrictions on their use. A new law in Hawaii, which went into effect in October, bans consumers from depositing cash into kiosks to buy cryptocurrency. The crackdown comes as scammers increasingly direct victims to cryptocurrency kiosks, often located in gas stations, convenience stores and grocery stores, to deposit cash that is converted into digital currency and transferred to accounts controlled by criminals. The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. Complaints increased 23% from the previous year, while financial losses jumped 58%, according to the agency’s cybercrime report, which was released in April. Older Americans have been particularly hard hit. More than half of the complaints involved people older than 50, who reported more than $302 million in losses last year. The mounting losses have prompted policymakers across the country to pursue tighter restrictions and outright bans on cryptocurrency kiosks — efforts that consumer advocates say are urgently needed to prevent further financial harm. “Every day that these laws aren’t passed are days where victims are having money stolen from them, and that money, because it’s through cryptocurrency and the nature of the kiosk, it’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back,” said Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director, in an interview with Stateline. Indiana became the first state to ban cryptocurrency kiosks in March, followed by Tennessee and Vermont in July and Minnesota in August. The measures mark a shift from earlier efforts to regulate the machines through transaction limits, fraud warnings and licensing requirements. items.body: After months of waiting, last week the Idaho State Tax Commission finally released information about which parents are receiving the $50 million in voucher money. Surprise, surprise, the Tax Commission report says most of the money is going to families that earn more than double the income of the average Idahoan and students who have never attended public schools. The average family that received voucher money this year earned $178,000, more than double the $84,234 of the average Idaho family. This makes the voucher program a government handout for families who can already afford to send their kids to private schools. Moreover, 75 percent of the families who took the money have never had their kids enrolled in a public school, even though advocates for the program promised that it would help students leave so-called “failing public schools” to attend private ones. And of the 25 percent of families whose kids did attend a public school, only 4.6 percent were enrolled for an entire school year a year ago. Critics of the voucher program warned that it would mainly benefit families living in urban areas rather than in rural communities. As expected, two thirds of the voucher money went to families living in just three counties – Ada, Canyon, and Kootenai. Furthermore, nearly 25 percent of the money went to only five private schools, most of them religious schools: Bishop Kelly High School in Boise, Cole Valley Christian in Meridian, Nampa Christian School, The Ambrose School in Meridian and Logos Classical Christian School in Moscow which is led by Christian Nationalist Doug Wilson. Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, a retired teacher, was one of the leading opponents of the voucher program and on Friday reacted to the Tax Commission report: “It’s hard enough for working parents to make ends meet without being asked to subsidize private school tuition for families who are better off than they are.” Ward-Engelking said someone should “explain to a rural parent why their child’s school can’t afford another teacher, but the state can afford to help a well-off family pay private school tuition. That’s a pretty lousy deal for rural Idaho.” Nothing in this report should be a surprise to Governor Brad Little or the legislators who voted to create the voucher program. They were warned that voucher programs across the country benefit the rich, and families that never sent their kids to public schools, and urban families over rural families. Still, Republican legislators, most of them rural, voted for vouchers and Governor Little signed it into law, even though 32,000 Idahoans contacted his office and asked him to veto the bill. Vouchers, which are unpopular among most citizens, was one of the major issues in the country during the recent mid-term election. The issue contributed to the election of Democratic governors and legislators in many Republican states which adopted vouchers. In Texas, longtime Republican Governor Greg Abbott, the leading advocate for school vouchers in the Lone Star State, lost to a Democrat who made her reputation by opposing vouchers while serving in the Legislature. In Arizona, voters not only re-elected Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs by a comfortable margin but elected a Democratic majority in both houses of the Arizona Legislature for the first time since 1966. In Iowa and Ohio, where Republican governors and legislators have expanded voucher programs, voters elected a Democratic governor for the first time in years. Unfortunately, in Idaho voters did not have a chance to weigh in on the voucher issue with accurate information about who it benefits. As a result, only one of the 62 Republican legislators who voted for the voucher bill lost their seat in the recent election. You cannot blame voters – they didn’t have the information on which to base their votes. As he moved toward his final step — completing his dissertation — the university rejected his proposal and entered an F grade. Morgan appealed the grade this spring. On April 29, the university acknowledged programmatic failures led to the failing grade and wiped it from his transcript, according to the claim. Interim program director Jaclyn Kettler wrote in an April 22 letter to the university’s registrar that “some program-level issues contributed to his challenges” with the course. The university hadn’t offered a key course on developing dissertation proposals when Morgan needed it because of a shortage of faculty available to teach it, Kettler wrote. “For reasons completely outside of his control, he was in a disadvantaged position in terms of his proposal development — making it harder to be successful in the course,” Kettler wrote. Program leadership and faculty turnover also contributed to the issue, Kettler said. Morgan needed to find a new dissertation chair and committee, which was “quite challenging” due to the number of faculty retiring or leaving the university. On April 30, the registrar approved removing the course from Morgan’s transcript, according to an email attached to the tort claim. The university is in the midst of merging the College of Education and School of Public Service. The merger, which will happen over the course of two years, won’t impact students, Andrew Finstuen, the interim dean, said this spring. The university did not respond to questions about the Public Policy and Administration PhD program. Morgan’s claim states that the university offered a transfer option that isn’t viable because Morgan would lose all the credits he already completed in the doctoral program. “Rather than correcting the structural issue by appointing a functional committee, the university administration left Claimant in a permanent academic blockade, offering only a disingenuous “transfer” that nullified years of labor and passing of comprehensive exams,” the claim reads. Morgan estimates lost wages of $1.5 million ($60,000 per year for 25 years as a non-tenure-track faculty member). He also estimates $15,000 in student loan-related losses.

items.body: The Idaho Tax Commission has released its first in-depth report on year one of the state’s new parental choice tax credit, and the overwhelming evidence shows it has been a monumental success. The analysis, released Friday, documents 12,216 final student awards, $49.3 million allocated for educational assistance, and awarded parent applications in every legislative district in Idaho. In addition, there are now 137 families on the tax credit waitlist. Those are substantial results for a program that has spent much of its early existence under political attack – from both legislators who have sought to defund it and activists who tried to knock it down in court. Both efforts proved unsuccessful. In full, the analysis gives Idaho a strong foundation on which to build—and good reason to focus on helping more families participate. The data shows that, of 6,875 awarded parents, 3,075 (or 44.7%) qualified under the program’s income priority, meaning their income on their 2024 return was at or below 300% of the federal poverty level. That number will vary based on household size. It includes families below the poverty line and families earning up to three times that threshold. Despite the claims that money would only be allocated to those living in Boise, Ada and Canyon counties account for just over half of awarded parents. More than 3,300 awarded parents—48% of the statewide total—are outside those two counties. They account for $22.64 million in educational assistance. In fact, on a per-capita basis, Idaho, Latah and Kootenai counties showed the largest participation rates. Eastern and southeastern Idaho provide another useful perspective, particularly given that most of the opposition to education choice came from those areas. Across the eight counties in that region, 647 parents were awarded help worth $4.27 million. Bannock and Bonneville counties alone account for 461 awarded parents and nearly $3 million. The report also shows families using different educational arrangements. Approximately one in five awarded students is homeschooling or planning to homeschool. The school table lists homeschool awards averaging approximately $2,776, accounting for about 19% of student awards but only 13% of award dollars. Separately, 3,092 awarded students—25.3%—had previously attended public school. Families are also reporting expenses beyond tuition. Although tuition accounts for 93.5% of expenses claimed to date, the remaining categories total approximately $2.5 million, including more than $1 million for curricula, approximately $600,000 for tutoring, $544,000 for transportation, and $246,000 for textbooks. These are practical expenses that every family may experience. There is no evidence of any Idaho parents submitting reimbursement requests for large screen TV’s or vacations. This is important to note given the prediction of opponents who claimed that funds would be abused. Now that we know the Idaho Parental Tax Credit to be such a roaring success, what should Idaho do with these findings? First, we should help approved families receive the assistance already allocated to them. The report identifies 430 parents who filed returns without claiming approved credits totaling $2.1 million. Some filed before receiving approval and may need to amend their returns. Second, we should examine the 1,232 applications that were started but not completed or submitted. Third, lawmakers should consider additional capacity. The current allocation averages approximately $4,038 per final student award. Holding that average and the current administrative share constant, a $75 million annual budget could help a total of approximately 18,300 students, about 6,100 more than current capacity. A $100 million budget could support some 24,400 students. Skeptics of Idaho’s Parental Choice Tax Credit have done everything possible to stop, obstruct and delay the program. items.body: Idaho’s private education tax credit is primarily subsidizing tuition for wealthy families whose children were already enrolled in a private school, according to a report released Friday. The Idaho State Tax Commission, for the first time, released a wide range of data that sheds light on the beneficiaries of the $50 million, taxpayer-funded Parental Choice Tax Credit program. GOP members of the Legislature and Republican Gov. Brad Little created the state’s first private school choice program last year through House Bill 93. Here are some of the highlights from the report: 12,216 students received a tax credit or advance payment. 80.7% attend a private school and 19.3% are home schooling. 74.7% have never attended a public school. $178,000 is the average adjusted gross income for recipient households. 1.7 is the average number of students per household that received a credit. 55.5% of households earn more and 44.5% earn less than 300% of the federal poverty level, a benchmark determining who had the first dibs on the credits. 93.5% of tax credits covered tuition expenses. In other words, the typical credit covered private school tuition for a family of four that earns $178,000 and whose children never attended a public school. Idaho’s median household income is $84,234, according to U.S. Census data. Friday’s report undermines a key selling point of the bitterly debated private school choice program: that it would help students who couldn’t otherwise afford private education options. “Idahoans were sold a lie about this voucher scheme,” House Minority Leader Ilana Rubel, D-Boise, said in a news release Friday. “We were told this program would help low-income children leave public schools for supposedly better-performing private schools. Instead, more than half of the families awarded tax credits are above the income threshold Republicans promised to prioritize, and nearly three-quarters of students have never attended an Idaho public school.” The refundable tax credit offers Idaho students, regardless of their family’s income, up to $5,000 — or $7,500 if they have special needs — to reimburse their non-public education costs, including tuition, curriculum and tutoring, among other things. Idaho Education News and others had sought data on the program’s rollout for months, but the Tax Commission denied records requests, promising a report by January. The agency ultimately published the report earlier than expected but 10 days after the Nov. 3 election, when all 105 state lawmakers and the governor were up for re-election. “Voters deserved this information before casting their ballots,” Rubel said. “We should repeal this program or, at the very least, end subsidies for higher-income families.” However, the report includes more data than HB 93 required. A provision in the bill told the Tax Commission to compile a report on the program’s first year with several data points. But it didn’t call for the percentage of students who previously attended a public school. In a statement Friday, Little said his administration “went above and beyond to provide as much information and data as possible while protecting taxpayers’ personal information.” “This report gives policymakers and the public a clearer picture of the program and provides the best available data to evaluate its effectiveness, identify opportunities for improvement, and ensure it continues to serve Idahoans well,” Little said in a news release. Emily Callihan, Little’s communications director, declined EdNews’ request to interview the governor Friday. EdNews also reached out to tax commissioner Janet Moyle along with Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog and House Majority Leader Jason Monks. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s Todd Achilles was one of a handful of major independent U.S. Senate candidates in red states to generate national attention ahead of the 2026 general election. Although he and the other high-profile independents lost their races, Achilles argues there’s still a future for independents to be a competitive alternative in a two-party system, and a viable way to win in such a Republican state. U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, talks to an Idaho News 6 reporter at the Idaho GOP election night watch party at the Grove in Boise, Idaho, on Nov. 8, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Achilles, a former Democratic state legislator, ended with 33.57% of the vote, compared to incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch’s 56.6% in the four-way race with no Democrat on the ballot. The other independent candidate, Natalie Fleming, received around 7% of the vote. In an election year where many Republicans struggled in nationwide federal races, Idaho voters stood by their GOP incumbents. “Idaho is different because, it’s just the advantage for Republicans among voter behavior is so outsized compared to even states in the South,” said Robert Jones, a partner and political strategist at Boise-based GS Strategy Group. Nearly 62% of Idaho voters are registered with the Republican Party, and 12% are registered Democrats, according to the Idaho secretary of state’s office . More than 24% aren’t affiliated with either party. Voters who deeply align with a major political party tend to stick with that party, even when they aren’t necessarily satisfied with their performance, said Idaho State University political scientist Edward Greer. Greer researches American politics, political psychology, and political behavior. “If a political party is not meeting those needs, then there’s not typically going to be a lot of crossover to the other side,” Greer said. “Usually, people will just kind of sit out.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. The win, although still comfortable, was Risch’s closest general election race since he first won his U.S. Senate seat in 2008. In 2008, Risch won with 57.7% of the vote against Democratic challenger and former congressman Larry LaRocco, who had 34.1% of the vote, with three other candidates on the ballot. Achilles, speaking to the Idaho Capital Sun the day after the election, said his campaign “built a great foundation” for the independent movement in Idaho. Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Todd Achilles speaks with attendees at an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, at Iconic Bistro and Bar in Garden City. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “We went from zero to 33% in 18 months,” he said. “… We got a lot of people excited. We had hundreds of meetings and town halls and events across the state. Everything I’m seeing in my inbox this morning is, ‘Let’s keep going.’ ‘We like what this independent movement is about.’” Achilles said he hasn’t decided if he would run again, but that he plans to continue to be involved in politics. His campaign garnered a similar share of votes as Democrats in other statewide races. Risch’s last challenger, Democrat Paulette Jordan, finished with a similar vote share, with 33.2% in the 2020 election. Brailsford wrote she agreed with Labrador’s interpretation of the law’s definition of “medical interventions,” writing that they refer to health actions that are “medical in nature.” “The (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) plainly and unambiguously sets out a standard of prohibited conduct that gives a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited,” Brailsford wrote. items.body: Idaho public school enrollment dropped by 8,983 students this fall, or 2.9% over the summer, according to data provided by the Idaho Department of Education. There are 304,871 students enrolled in schools across Idaho, down from 313,854 at the end of last school year. This is the largest enrollment drop in at least 10 years, and the drop continues a yearslong trend. A number of factors can impact school enrollment, from birth rates to home prices to school choice. The biggest winners — charter schools, which gained nearly a thousand students, propelled by the fall opening of seven. The biggest losers — traditional districts, including Idaho’s largest West Ada. The Boise School district, Idaho’s second largest, continued its years-long losing trend with a drop of more than 1,000. All but 15 of 117 districts lost students. Virtual schools, either charters or those governed by districts, also showed big losses. The migration away from virtual schools and possibly to homeschooling or private schools coincides with the first year of the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit, which 12,561 students applied for. The funds, up to $5,000 per student or $7,500 for a student with special needs, can be used to cover homeschooling costs and private school tuition. But very little is known about who received the tax credit, after requests for demographic data were denied. Enrollment numbers change throughout the year as students move and schools correct data inputs. Districts report enrollment to the state monthly. EdNews compared 2026 spring counts to this fall for this story. Enrollment change varies by age and school type Idaho’s enrollment decline is concentrated among elementary students, while enrollment continues to grow in middle and high schools, EdNews reported earlier this year. Idaho’s population continues to increase, with over 2 million residents statewide, but just 8% of growth is attributed to school-aged children, according to Idaho Department of Labor Economist Lisa Grigg. Charter schools showed a net gain of about 515 students. New charter schools accounted for 2,124 students, ranging from 658 at Brabion Academy to 14 at Trailhead Virtual Academy. The largest charter enrollment loss was at Idaho Home Learning Academy, with 742 students. IHLA came under fire last legislative session after a report found payments to families of up to $1,800 were spent inappropriately. Payments have more guardrails on how they’re spent this year. At the same time, families could apply for a larger tax credit to homeschool. Virtual public schools received a $3 million funding cut last session. Enrollment in both charter and district-run online schools dropped last year. Quick facts: 39 of 82 charter schools gained or maintained enrollment. 43 charter schools lost enrollment. 15 of 117 traditional public school districts gained or maintained enrollment. 102 traditional districts lost enrollment. items.body: Two music teachers are orchestrating the resistance to artificial intelligence in Idaho. Boise couple Jack and Cathryn Gardner have organized the state’s first AI protest. They’ve been meeting with federal and state lawmakers to push for regulations on the technology, and they’re seeing firsthand how AI influences young students. Cathryn teaches music to elementary students in the Boise School District and Jack, who formerly taught music in the Nampa School District, is a freelance bassist teaching private lessons to high school and college students. “I see it affecting how my students are thinking critically and thinking cognitively,” Cathryn told Idaho Education News in an interview last month. “But I’m seeing, too, that it’s affecting their ability to process and to work independently and to think creatively.” Jack and Cathryn co-lead the Boise chapter of PauseAI US . The nationwide advocacy group’s goal is to tighten government regulation on AI development to prevent “adversarial superintelligence,” rogue AI agents that disobey humans. The couple holds monthly meetups and tables weekly at community events. Their first protest, held Oct. 24 in front of the Idaho Statehouse, included speeches from volunteers and signs and flyers advocating for humanism, reported The Arbiter, Boise State University’s campus newspaper. Meanwhile, Jack and Cathryn have been meeting with lawmakers, including U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson and Sen. Jim Risch, to advocate for regulations on AI. They’ve been featured in The New York Times . PauseAI US leaders consider the couple their “best organizers,” and praise their ability to break down complex AI concerns for people without technical knowledge. “ I think they’re a great example of like, yeah, any person can go meet with the senator, raise the alarm, and propose some good ideas, and together we can solve the problem,” said Alvaro Cuba, associate director at PauseAI. Jack Gardner, left, with U.S. Senator Jim Risch. (Jack Gardner photo) Music teachers grow concerned with AI Making music is one of the few remaining activities that only humans can do, Jack said, a nd a s artificial intelligence proliferates education and the workforce, the Gardners are putting humanity at the center of their lessons. “ AI noise isn’t really music,” Jack said. “…Studying an instrument teaches delayed gratification, which is the polar opposite of what AI promises and doesn’t deliver. Being in an ensemble teaches you human interaction skills that they’re not getting in their online lives.” When it comes to AI’s broader impact on society, Jack had been focused on the technology stealing musicians’ work without credit or compensation. Then, last year, he learned about the hypothesis that AI’s progress could lead to the extinction of humanity. This summer, rogue AI agents made real-life headlines after OpenAI’s agents breached containment and hacked Hugging Face , an open-source AI development platform. Jack knew he had to do something about it. He and Cathryn searched for anti-AI organizations and joined Pause AI in August of 2025. They founded PauseAI Boise shortly after. items.body: School trustees want Idaho to bring its K-12 funding model into the 21 st century. No, really, they do. Convening in Boise last week, the state’s school trustees overwhelmingly passed three different resolutions calling for changes to a much-maligned and aging school funding formula, which was last modified in 1994. The trustees aren’t alone. State superintendent Debbie Critchfield, easily re-elected to a second term last week, has made a funding formula rewrite her top priority. But the big question mark is still Gov. Brad Little, also easily re-elected last week. In his first two terms, Little has supported Idaho’s current school funding approach, while keeping his options open. Any funding formula rewrite must go through Little. Predictably enough, Little isn’t committing himself. For those just checking in — or those who need a refresher — here’s a summary of the debate, and what’s at stake. Attendance vs. enrollment The formula has long been based on student attendance. And Little has been on board with this status quo approach. Supporters of an attendance-based model want schools to have an incentive to get (and keep) kids in classroom seats. Supporters of a rewrite, such as Critchfield, point out that those kids in the seats are fundamentally different. It costs more to teach a special education student, an English language learner, or a gifted and talented student. They also point out that students are more mobile than they were in 1994 — more likely to split up their schedule, instead of spending their entire day in one building. Hence the argument for an enrollment-based model that reflects individual student needs and student schedules. The funding formula drives the largest distribution of dollars in the state budget — the $2.8 billion in tax revenues that go out to K-12 schools. The high stakes help explain why elected officials and education lobbyists have haggled over a rewrite for a decade. items.body: Next year marks the second consecutive year of double digit premium rate increases across Your Health Idaho plans. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images) For about the next month, Idahoans can enroll in health insurance plans on the state’s exchange. As health insurance premiums continue to grow, Idaho’s exchange, Your Health Idaho, is the only place that Idahoans can go to get private health insurance discounted by the federal government. For some Idahoans, that discount — in the form of a tax credit — might shield them from the average of 12% premium rises for plans on the exchange, said Your Health Idaho Executive Director Pat Kelly. That’s because the tax credit is linked to the cost of one slate of plans, the silver, he said. “We’re actually seeing net premiums — which is the amount consumers pay after the tax credit is applied — we’re seeing those net premiums either flat or declining in 2027,” Kelly said in an interview. He offered a few examples of how that could work. A single person in Ada County earning $36,000 a year might pay $8 less in premiums. If that person lived in the Magic Valley, they might pay $30 less in premiums, he said. “Health insurance, for those that receive a tax credit, is an incredible affordability story this year,” Kelly said. “They’re actually seeing plans that are either the same net premium cost from ‘26 to ‘27, or actually a decrease, which is just unheard of these days.” But he stressed that the tax credit’s application depends on your family’s specifics: Where you live, how big your household is, and how much you make. So he encouraged Idahoans to use Your Health Idaho’s online tool to estimate how much of a tax credit they’d receive. Congress last year didn’t renew bigger discounts on federal and state exchanges, but there are still smaller discounts baked into the federal Affordable Care Act, which led to the exchanges’ creation. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits last year led about 25,000 Idahoans to cancel plans on the state exchange, Your Health Idaho estimated. Next year marks the second consecutive year of double digit premium rate increases across Your Health Idaho plans. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE When is open enrollment? And how do I sign up and shop around? Open enrollment for Your Health Idaho lasts until Dec. 15. The cutoff that day is 11:59 p.m. Mountain time. Coverage for new plans starts Jan. 1. On the exchange, Idahoans can pick from 143 medical plans and 32 dental plans from 12 insurance companies. At the state exchange’s website , you can shop for plans, see how much in a tax credit you could qualify for, use an affordability tool and find an agent or broker who can help you free of cost. Find pop-up enrollment centers hosted by Your Health Idaho online . Your Health Idaho officials say you shouldn’t wait until the last minute to enroll. For the most part, open enrollment is the last time that Idahoans can enroll in Your Health Idaho before next fall, unless they have a qualifying life event . “Start early, bring your questions, and let a local expert help you find coverage that fits your life and your budget,” Marcia Benton, a broker in Meridian, said in a written statement. (Photo by Christophe Paul/U.S. Department of Agriculture) Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest resting place for America’s heroes, is sacred ground for our veterans. As we commemorate Veterans Day this year, we should turn our thoughts and pay our respects to the many Idahoans who have been laid to rest in that hallowed ground. They include two Congressional Medal of Honor winners. Col. Reginald Rodney Myers , who was born in Boise, earned the Medal of Honor for valor in the vicious Battle of Chosin Reservoir in Korea in November of 1950. First Lt. Vernon J. Baker, who was born in Wyoming, but lived his last 15 years in Idaho, received the Medal of HOnor for conspicuous valor near Viareggio, Italy, in April of 1945. His award came 52 years late because of his black skin. A number of Idahoans from Vietnam and subsequent wars are interred in the peaceful environs of Arlington. In July of 2012, the remains of Chief Master Sgt. Larry Thornton of Idaho Falls were buried at Arlington , 45 years after his AC-47D took off from Vietnam on Christmas Eve of 1965 and disappeared over Laos. I’ve been to Arlington many times since my Vietnam service. Every time I saw the grave marker of a Vietnam comrade, I was flooded with profound grief and anger for the 58,220 American lives taken by that ill-fated war, including 251 with Idaho connections. Those emotions were always somewhat assuaged by the quiet, dignified atmosphere of the cemetery. That calming atmosphere is currently facing a serious threat from another Donald Trump vanity project. Trump’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch will sit smack dab in front of Arlington Cemetery, destroying its peace and tranquility, as well as the symmetry and symbolism of its location. The National Park Service dared to report that the arch “would break alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House that was Robert E. Lee’s home.” It continued: “The bridge alignment and associated ceremonial landscape were intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River.” It has also been noted that the arch requires an act of Congress. It does not have congressional approval, but that has never stopped Trump from bullying ahead. Trump is not the first president to propose construction that would have severely interfered with that alignment, as well as the pastoral atmosphere of the cemetery. President Franklin D. Why build an arch in the first place? The Romans were among the first of the ancients to construct triumphal arches. They made an art of building arches to recognize victorious generals returning from battle. It is not clear why Trump would be entitled to an arch on that basis because his Iran War has been an unmitigated disaster for our country. The Iranians have kept what remains of their nuclear material. The war has caused skyrocketing prices for gas, diesel, fertilizer, and most consumer goods that need to be transported. After the hearing, the Boise City Council voted unanimously to approve a six-month moratorium in new large data center projects. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) A standing-room-only crowd of more than 100 people applauded after the Boise City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to place a six-month moratorium on the construction of large new data centers. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The moratorium went into effect immediately, and applies to all data center projects that are 100,000 square-feet or larger, or use 20 megawatts of power. Passing the moratorium means Boise will not accept or process any applications for large data centers that fall within the moratorium’s parameters. “It’s a six-month moratorium that will put the brakes on hyperscale data centers in Boise, so it gives us the time to better determine and understand the impacts that these will have,” said Boise Mayor Lauren McLean, who proposed the moratorium Friday. McLean said the city does not currently have any large data center applications pending. “I’m doing this now before we have an application so that we can be sure that we get it right,” McLean said. Boise city officials will use the moratorium to review code and policies, study the impact on water, energy use, wastewater, noise and public safety, and gather public feedback. Chief of Staff Hannah Brass Greer said Boise’s existing code does not address data centers. “One of the things we would be doing is looking at our code and where it would fit and what restrictions or guidelines we want to put in place,” Brass Greer said. The Boise City Council approved the emergency moratorium following an approximately one-hour public hearing during its meeting Tuesday at Boise City Hall. ‘Don’t sell off our future to the highest bidder’: Public testimony supported the pause Need to get in touch? items.body: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images) Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has survived an impeachment effort, at least for now, after the U.S. House on Tuesday blocked a vote over charges that the Cabinet official oversaw extrajudicial killings and an illegal war against Iran. The House voted 211-204 , largely along party lines, to refer articles of impeachment against Hegseth to a committee — effectively killing the impeachment effort until the end of the current Congress in January. Eleven Democrats and seven Republicans missed the vote. The vote came hours after Hegseth defended himself in a fiery news conference at the Pentagon, where he denounced the impeachment effort as an attack on American service members. He called the bid to remove him a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term. “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said. Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the Defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges. Impeachment would have represented an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon. On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. Hegseth’s opponents could try again to impeach him during the new Congress, which begins in January. Democrats will hold a large majority in the House at that time. Earlier in the day, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who will likely become majority leader when his party takes over the chamber, said Hegseth should stand trial in the Senate if impeached. “Hegseth is already trying to hide behind our troops, falsely claiming that Congress disapproves of our courageous servicemembers even though we have fought to bring them home for months,” Schumer said. President Donald Trump has so far stood by Hegseth. He praised the Defense secretary in multiple public remarks over the past two weeks, saying he’s “done a fantastic job” in reducing the number of “woke” four-star generals, and for conducting the “war with Venezuela,” which he said “was over in 48 minutes.” “Pete Hegseth should be praised, not Impeached. Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday.

items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at Borah High School in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A week after the midterm election, Idaho election officials reported more than 300 ballots went uncounted on election night in an eastern Idaho county. The Office of the Idaho Secretary of State on Tuesday afternoon announced that 333 uncounted ballots had been identified during a post-election review in one precinct in Bannock County. State election officials said no outcomes changed once the ballots had been counted. The votes will be added to the state’s election results website Tuesday, officials added. Election recount planned in North Idaho county that didn’t report 2,300 ballots “Once again, this demonstrates the importance of the reconciliation process we use to verify election results following every election,” Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican who was reelected as the state’s top election official, said in a written statement. “While I am thankful that these ballots were identified, we will be working to determine why these ballots were not processed on election night and working with counties across the state to reinforce our election processes.” This is at least the second Idaho county to report it left some ballots unreported in election results after last week’s election. State election officials on Tuesday were overseeing a recount of ballots in North Idaho’s Latah County , after the county reported more than 2,300 ballots went unreported in election results. Miller ordered Idaho State Police and Idaho Department of Correction to release information about officers’ employment history, including the dates of their employment and the reason for their separation. (InvestigateWest illustration) This article originally published in InvestigateWest on Nov. 10. Idaho State Police and the Idaho Department of Correction improperly withheld police employment records and other information from two news organizations, according to a state court ruling ordering the information be released. InvestigateWest and the Invisible Institute sued the state agencies on June 16 for allegedly concealing information about officers’ employment histories that were previously disclosed to the news outlets. InvestigateWest used officer employment records to expose alleged sexual misconduct by dozens of Idaho prison guards in an October 2025 series , and to show how many were allowed to resign without facing other disciplinary action or criminal prosecution. The reporting prompted Idaho lawmakers to remove a loophole in a sexual abuse law that made it more difficult for prosecutors to charge prison staff, and to order an independent review of how the women’s prison system handles reports of sexual abuse. After those stories were published, reporters from InvestigateWest and the Invisible Institute sought updated officer employment records, but the Department of Correction and state police denied those requests, stating that they would no longer disclose whether an officer retired, resigned or was fired. A records clerk also told the Invisible Institute that Idaho State Police leadership decided to “disable” a tool that allowed them to search an internal employment database. In a Nov. 5 ruling, Ada County District Judge Patrick J. Miller ordered the state agencies to release information about officers’ employment history, including the dates of their employment and the reason for their separation. That includes information about two former prison guards accused of sexually assaulting an inmate, who described the assaults and the mental toll it took on her to an InvestigateWest reporter. “This ruling is a win for government transparency — and accountability — in Idaho,” said Jacob Fries, InvestigateWest’s executive director. “These public records had been essential to our reporter’s work, which led directly to a new state law helping protect incarcerated people from abuses of power.” State law broadly defines “employment history” to include the entire course of a person’s employment, from when it started to the nature of how it ended, Judge Miller wrote, concluding that whether someone was terminated, retired or resigned is public information. The agencies argued that disclosing an officer was terminated, for example, would suggest potential disciplinary action against the individual, and that legislators specifically exempted disciplinary details from disclosure. Idaho State Police also claimed the requested employment history information was contained in confidential decertification files that it said are exempt. Judge Miller said disclosing the reason for separation doesn’t amount to revealing the underlying details behind an employee’s departure. And just because an officer’s employment history and dates of service are in the same file as confidential details doesn’t mean they “lose their character” as disclosable records, the judge wrote. The Idaho Public Records Act “does not categorically shield every piece of information contained within an otherwise exempt file. To hold otherwise would permit an agency to withhold nonexempt employment-history information based solely upon the location in which it is maintained,” according to the ruling. items.body: Sierra Bohamera is all about algorithms. Both in her math classroom at Capital High School, and on TikTok, where she shares her life and lessons to her 500,000 followers. Growing up in Bend, Ore., Bohamera always loved school. Teachers were the people she looked up to in life. “I thought they were the coolest people ever,” Bohamera said. “They made me feel very welcome in class and inspired to try.” As a high schooler, Bohamera interned at a local elementary school and was hooked. She moved to Idaho to attend Boise State University. She student taught in kindergarten and loved it. But a second student teaching experience in her minor subject area, math, proved to be transformative. Bohamera struggled in math until the fifth grade, when she had a teacher who let her make mistakes then helped her work through the issue to get the right answer. At the time, Bohamera was shy and the teacher would encourage her to “share your thinking with the class.” That experience taught Bohamera she can do hard things and it’s a moment she still thinks about 20 years later. Still, Bohamera didn’t see herself as solely a math teacher, so she was shocked to find she enjoyed working with teenagers. She loved the challenge of earning older students’ trust, especially when they come in a bit apprehensive. “Math can be intimidating for kids,” Bohamera said. “A lot of times if they don’t get it right away they feel like they’re dumb.” Now in her eighth year at Capital High, “Miss Bo,” as she’s known, focuses on making class fun. Instead of a worksheet with practice problems, students compete in groups to solve problems quickly. “All of a sudden they’ve done 20 problems,” Bohamera said. “They want to get the right answer so they can beat the other team.” She focuses on positive reinforcement, building on individual students’ strengths to tackle problems they may struggle with. The goal is to teach students not just math, but that they can do hard things, Bohamera said. The students love Bohamera, said Principal Derek Gardner, in part because she connects with them. “It’s not just a math class where you put your head down and are working by yourself sort of the more traditional way,” Gardner said. “It’s almost the exact opposite of that.” It’s rarely quiet when Gardner walks by Bohamera’s room. “It’s a very productive noise,” he said. Click to view slideshow. Part of that connection comes from Bohamera’s goal of being a role model both in and out of the classroom, he said. Since 2021, Bohamera has posted on TikTok about her life as a teacher. She posts teacher outfits, lesson ideas, and her adventures around Boise as “ThatTrendyTeacher.” She garnered more than 500,000 followers on TikTok and another few hundred thousand on Instagram. “I initially downloaded it because I wanted to connect more with students,” Bohamera said. But she quickly saw other teachers posting and decided it looked fun. Her hope now is to show her followers and students what a well rounded lifestyle is with a good work life balance. “I always kind of post with the lense of my student is watching and my school is watching,” Bohamera said. “When you grow up, and if you want to do similar things, you can see a positive adult role model in your life.” Especially at a time when there can be negativity online about the profession and public schools, Bohamera hopes to show people that there are teachers who love their job and have fun doing it. The goal for Bohamera is to make her class about more than math; it’s about life. The old adage, “I’ll never use this in real life,” doesn’t bother Bohamera. “I tell them that even if it’s not the exact math concept in real life, you’re going to use those problem-solving skills,” she said. “These skills that I’m teaching you in math can be transferable to any job.” Sierra Bohamera Years Teaching: 10 Grades Taught: 8, 10-12 What advice would you give to new teachers? “You don’t have to be perfect, I know that you want everything to be perfect but th
