(Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images) U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone Tuesday as he faces potential impeachment by the U.S. House of Representatives this week, casting the effort as an attack on American service members. Hegseth during a rare news conference at the Pentagon called the impeachment effort a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term. “Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said. The House, led by Republicans during the lame-duck session following the Nov. 3 election, is set to vote on impeaching Hegseth as soon as Wednesday, with a procedural vote expected later Tuesday. Massie impeachment articles Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges. Impeachment would represent an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Democrats, as well as some Republicans, are expected to support the effort, raising the possibility the articles will pass and trigger a trial in the Senate, though the outcome is unclear there. Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon. On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger. “It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said. Drug boats Massie told reporters on Monday that Hegseth’s conduct of the military has endangered Americans. Hegseth has denied ordering the strike, but said he supported it. The building needs an estimated $5.4 million in repairs and updates within 10 years. Some grade levels at the school have one class. Trustee Meghan Brown said small is good when intentional, but it can lead to low morale. She said her kids used to attend a school that had a grade level with one class. items.body: Boise State University is shifting millions of dollars into its athletics programs to protect a “truly global” brand, President David Hahn says. The funding shift could also allow Boise State to ride through a turbulent time in college sports — where schools can now spend up to $21.6 million in “revenue sharing” payments to student athletes. “The landscape has changed so rapidly,” Hahn said in the latest edition of The EdNews Show . “It’s an arms race.” The State Board of Education is allowing Boise State to use reserves to cover up to $18 million in athletics deficits. Hahn hopes the short-term plan will buy Boise State some “stability,” as Congress considers an overhaul of college athletics. Meanwhile, he’s hoping to preserve Boise State’s athletics brand — which introduces Boise State to prospective applicants and donors. “Brands take decades and years to build, and they can be lost very quickly,” he said. “That brand has value far beyond the number of tickets we sell on a Saturday afternoon.” Hahn discussed several other topics in the EdNews interview. Here are a couple of quick highlights: Enrollment . Boise State’s fall student numbers are up, slightly. But with Idaho’s college-aged population likely to grow in future years — and with other states bracing for a population decrease — Boise State will face increased competition to recruit and retain in-state students. Boise State’s affordability and campus environment — and its athletics brand — are all potential selling points. “(We need to) be all we can be,” Hahn said. The political climate . Hahn, hired on July 1, said he is encouraged by his early conversations with legislators. The relationship between Boise State and the Legislature has been contentious for several years — resulting in budget cuts driven by skepticism about the university’s social justice agenda. But Hahn said the university is poised to capitalize on growth in Idaho, and especially in the Treasure Valley. “It’s our moment … and my job is to build the relationships, find that common ground. And it’s been going well.” This edition of the EdNews Show — and all previous episodes — are available on YouTube , Spotify or Apple Podcasts .

items.body: (UPDATED, 4:46 p.m., with more national context on Idaho’s funding decrease.) Idaho’s share of federal healthcare grants will decrease next year. The reasons for the reduction are unclear — and it’s too early to know how the cut will affect Idaho programs. In the second year of the feds’ five-year, $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program , Idaho will receive close to $182.7 million. Idaho’s first-year grant totaled $185.9 million. In a news release Monday, Gov. Brad Little’s office announced the Year Two grants — which could have far-reaching implications for K-12 and higher education programs. But the news release made no mention of the reduction. Little’s office has received no explanation of the reduction, spokeswoman Emily Callihan told EdNews in an email Monday afternoon. The state Department of Health and Welfare had no answers either, spokesman AJ McWhorter said Monday afternoon. The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services did not immediately respond to questions from EdNews. Idaho’s funding decrease comes to slightly more than $3.25 million — ranking as one of the steepest in the nation. Only nine states lost more healthcare grant dollars from Year One to Year Two. For months, state officials have said Idaho’s healthcare grant could increase — or decrease. The feds set up a competitive program, tying future payments to states’ track records. A state that met the feds’ deadlines and paperwork requirements could receive additional funding, at the expense of states that struggled. But Idaho met the feds’ Year One deadline. Idaho committed its $185.9 million in grants on Oct. 28, a couple of days ahead of schedule. More than $25 million of the first-year money will go to education-related programs: The biggest chunk, $12.5 million, will go into nearly a dozen “healthcare career advancement track” programs. Most of these projects are cooperative efforts involving two or more colleges and universities. All are designed to support rural students considering careers in healthcare fields. Another $8 million will go into fellowships and residencies, placing medical school graduates in rural Idaho. The University of Idaho will receive or share an additional $4.8 million in grants, Idaho State University will receive $2 million and Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and the Blind will receive nearly $900,000 for a mobile pediatric clinic. Decisions about spending the reduced grant will fall to a state agency in transition — and a legislative committee also facing a shakeup. Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron is stepping down later this year. An eight-member legislative committee is overseeing the grants; two committee members, Republican Reps. Dori Healey of Boise and Dustin Manwaring of Pocatello, were ousted in last week’s election . For Health and Welfare, the work is just getting started. “The (rural healthcare) program is in the process of reviewing the award and will be working with CMS to update the program’s workplan and budget,” McWhorter said Monday.

items.body: Arlington National Cemetery, the nation’s largest resting place for America’s heroes, is sacred ground for our veterans. As we commemorate Veterans Day this year, we should turn our thoughts and pay our respects to the many Idahoans who have been laid to rest in that hallowed ground. They include two Congressional Medal of Honor winners. Colonel Reginald Rodney Myers , who was born in Boise, earned the MOH for valor in the vicious Battle of Chosin Reservoir in Korea in November of 1950. First Lieutenant Vernon J. Baker, who was born in Wyoming, but lived his last 15 years in Idaho, received the MOH for conspicuous valor near Viareggio, Italy, in April of 1945. His award came 52 years late because of his black skin. A number of Idahoans from Vietnam and subsequent wars are interred in the peaceful environs of Arlington. In July of 2012, the remains of Chief Master Sgt. Larry Thornton of Idaho Falls were buried at Arlington , 45 years after his AC-47D took off from Vietnam on Christmas Eve of 1965 and disappeared over Laos. I’ve been to Arlington many times since my Vietnam service. Every time I saw the grave marker of a Vietnam comrade, I was flooded with profound grief and anger for the 58,220 American lives taken by that ill-fated war, including 251 with Idaho connections. Those emotions were always somewhat assuaged by the quiet, dignified atmosphere of the Cemetery. That calming atmosphere is currently facing a serious threat from another Donald Trump vanity project. Trump’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch will sit smack dab in front of Arlington Cemetery, destroying its peace and tranquility, as well as the symmetry and symbolism of its location. The National Park Service dared to report that the arch “would break alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House that was Robert E. Lee’s home.” It continued: “The bridge alignment and associated ceremonial landscape were intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River.” It has also been noted that the arch requires an Act of Congress. It does not have Congressional approval, but that has never stopped Trump from bullying ahead. Trump is not the first president to propose construction that would have severely interfered with that alignment, as well as the pastoral atmosphere of the Cemetery. President Franklin D. Roosevelt proposed building the Pentagon in that location. He changed his mind after being convinced that it would obliterate the backdrop of tiered headstones and Arlington House. Why build an arch in the first place? The Romans were among the first of the ancients to construct triumphal arches. They made an art of building arches to recognize victorious generals returning from battle. It is not clear why Trump would be entitled to an arch on that basis because his Iran War has been an unmitigated disaster for our country. The Iranians have kept what remains of their nuclear material. The war has caused skyrocketing prices for gas, diesel, fertilizer, and most consumer goods that need to be transported. The explanation for the arch must lie elsewhere. Trump admitted last October that the monument was intended to honor “me” but later claimed it was to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. As he has continued to take flak for the project, Trump and his lackeys now contend it is required for the national defense. We already have a national defense project in the grand ballroom adjacent to the White House, but that does not seem to be sufficient in the president’s mind. In a shameful attempt to get around building restrictions, he now claims the arch will be laden with drones, snipers and machine guns so as to protect Washington from attack. If he had the slightest understanding of military tactics, he would understand that his arch would make an indefensible sitting-duck target. Not everyone is keen for Trump’s vanity arch. Federal authorities said on Monday Idaho will receive about $182.7 million in the second year of a grant designed to improve rural healthcare, marking a reduction from Idaho’s first-year award. The federal Rural Health Transformation grant was part of the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, in which Congress allocated $50 billion nationwide for the five-year program. Idaho was awarded nearly $186 million on Dec. 30, 2025, for the first year of the program. Idaho’s Republican Gov. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at the Calvary Baptist Church in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho, a Republican stronghold, the closest Democrat in this year’s election to securing a seat in Congress or statewide office was 11 points behind. The candidate, Ellie Gilbreath, was trying to stop Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson’s bid for reelection to a 15th term. Across the country last week, Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress , won governorships in most states and made headway in state legislatures . Amid national blue wave, Idaho Democrats gain six legislative seats — flipping competitive districts But by the time the national blue wave — or tsunami, as some are calling it — hit Idaho, the tide had turned it into a ripple. Idaho Democrats made modest gains. They swept full control of three legislative districts, gaining six more legislative seats , a shift that does little to chip away at Republicans’ supermajority control of the Legislature. And a closer look at election results shows that across the board, Democrats captured slightly more votes against Republican incumbents in statewide office and congress , who easily won reelection. But in all of those races, Democratic victory was still far off. No Democrat has won a statewide office in the state since 2002, and the last Democratic congressman in Idaho served in 2010. If Democrats want to upset decades of Idaho political history by winning a top of the ticket race, they have a long way to go. On average, Democrats gained 6 points of the vote share in federal and state races compared to the last time those offices were up for election. Still, Idaho Democrats this year were an average of 27 points behind Republicans, according to an analysis of election results by the Idaho Capital Sun. Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler wasn’t surprised that the blue wave didn’t carry Democrats through in Idaho. “Idaho is a solidly Republican state. We don’t tend to see too many competitive races” in the general election for statewide races, she said in an interview. “ … It’s just solid enough Republican that it’s hard for even a blue wave in other areas of the country to have too much influence, especially for those statewide races.” The Idaho Democratic Party also boasted another gain: Democrats got more of the vote in 67 legislative races than they did in 2024. This year’s election results are unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24. items.body: Dozens of school trustees were granted an impromptu session with Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron on Wednesday to discuss the collapse of an employee health insurance program. Nothing has changed — they all had to pay their share of the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s $13 million shortfall — but they had the opportunity to get some questions answered during their annual Idaho School Boards Association conference in Boise. Cameron provided some new details about what happened to the trust, as his department is conducting an investigation that is expected to wrap up this month. Those managing the trust set rates too low and were counting on a “hope, a wing and a prayer” to get through the latest benefit year. Instead, their plan didn’t work. The trust became insolvent and a district court judge has taken all authority away from the trust’s leaders and granted full power to Cameron to rehabilitate the benefit trust. “The nightmare took place really over a couple-year period of time,” Cameron said. “The trust had assumed the risk, and the risk occurred.” Sen.-elect Soñia Galaviz, D-Boise, asked Cameron to speak at the ISBA conference and said he had to rearrange his schedule to attend. The hourlong presentation and Q&A on Wednesday was tacked on to the end of the day’s scheduled events. Attendees were informed about it at lunchtime. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho, more than a third of votes in Tuesday’s election were cast before Election Day. Over 290,000 of the more than 731,000 ballots cast in the election were through early and absentee voting, according to data from the Idaho secretary of state’s office. That’s 100,000 more of those types of voting than were submitted during the state’s last election for statewide offices in 2022, according to the state election agency. Those forms of voting — available without a need to state a reason — allow voters to cast ballots either in person or by mail before Election Day. (Technically, some of these absentee ballots were submitted on Election Day. In Idaho, absentee ballots may be submitted until polls close at 8 p.m. local time on Election Day.) Superior Court judge has ordered the Idaho National Guard to produce documents related to an incident in May in which guards members detained a woman outside her home. D.C. resident Anna King filed a separate $3 million claim against the Idaho National Guard in July for injuries and distress she said she experienced when she was detained on May 8. Members of the Gem State’s National Guard have been in the nation’s Capital since February as part of a Joint Task Force, although there was no public announcement of the deployment until after King filed her claim, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. National Guard and U.S. Department of Defense will have to produce, or explain why they can’t produce, documents related to the detainment of King. King wrote in her tort claim against the Idaho National Guard that the troops did not explain why they were detaining her or provide a warrant when they approached her that evening. A video of the incident shows three men in National Guard uniforms approaching King, who had been sitting on a bench outside her apartment. King told the guards members not to touch her. She walked toward the steps to go back into her apartment, but the troops blocked her, the video showed. Two of them pinned her against the ground and secured her wrists behind her back. The U.S. government charged King with two counts of misdemeanor assault on a police officer on May 9. In August, the U.S. Attorney’s Office added three more charges of simple assault. The charges stem from alleged assaults on May 6. King pleaded not guilty and asked for a trial. King’s attorney, Jeffrey Nestler, said the Idaho National Guard provided one document, but the legal team felt it wasn’t sufficient. King’s attorneys asked for all reports, records, communications, directives and other documents from the Idaho National Guard related to King. Di Toro agreed, and ordered the prosecutor to ensure the entities produce relevant documents. According to court documents and Nestler, the Idaho National Guard members who detained King on May 8 said they had “prior run-ins” with King and had been ordered to detain her. “We’re here now in the part of the law that requires the government to do more than just ask questions, so I’m going to direct you to actually spend a little more time trying to understand whether prior to May 6, the Idaho National Guard had what the defense is calling a run-in with Ms. King,” Di Toro told Assistant United States Attorney Vanessa Jacobsen Thursday. King is a former Army captain and Purple Heart and Bronze Star recipient, according to a press release announcing her tort claim. “As a trained combat veteran, I never imagined that armed National Guard members would attack, injure, and traumatize me at my home,” King said in the press release. “We are not at war with Americans, and my porch is not a war zone.” The trial in the case against King is scheduled to start July 27, 2027. items.body: The Idaho School Boards Association passed nine resolutions at its annual meeting on Friday, urging the 2027 Legislature to preserve local control and fulfill its constitutional responsibility to provide adequate funding for all public schools. School board members from across the state gathered in Boise to elect leadership, approve bylaws and pass resolutions that will guide the association’s lobbying efforts throughout the coming legislative session. “The ISBA legislative platform gives our association a unified voice as we advocate for Idaho public schools,” said outgoing President Jason Sevy, a Marsing trustee. With a bang of his gavel at the end of Friday’s general session, Sevy ended his time as president and handed the reins over to Eric Smallwood, chair of the Twin Falls school board, who has served as president-elect for the past year. Members elected Brett Plummer of Challis as the new president-elect and Pam Wagoner of Middleton as vice president. They were the only candidates for each position. Click to view slideshow. “My priorities are clear: Strengthening board collaboration across the districts,” Plummer said in a prepared speech before the vote. “We’re stronger when we share ideas, resources and solutions.” But the main event on Friday was voting on eight pre-submitted resolutions and one introduced on the floor that addressed the Idaho School Benefit Trust shortfall . They all passed. Votes are weighted based on the size of the district and are not a direct one-to-one correlation with the number of trustees. Here’s the ISBA’s new legislative platform. Resolution No. 1: Human growth and development video Submitted by the Boise School District Passed: 8,866-112 (98.7%) Boise trustee Paul Bennion presented a resolution that asks the Legislature to clean up “conflicting and impractical” language around human growth and development instruction, in particular a requirement to show a fetal development video in classrooms. Public schools have had one year to implement a law — enacted through Senate Bill 1046 in 2025 — requiring that students in grades 5-12 watch a high-definition ultrasound video during instruction on human growth and development. items.body: Enrollment in college-level courses provided by the Idaho Digital Learning Alliance fell 46% in summer and fall 2026 compared with the same period last year, as new fees took effect after a major cut to the state-funded online learning program. In the summer and fall of 2025, IDLA recorded 5,540 dual credit enrollments. In 2026, it recorded 2,980 dual credit enrollments in the same time period. IDLA Superintendent Jeff Simmons discussed the decline during a Thursday workshop at the Idaho School Boards Association’s annual convention in Boise. A decline in funding has forced IDLA to draw on its savings to serve more students than the program is funded to accommodate. “That’s certainly not something we can do every year,” Simmons said of using savings to serve more students than its funding allows. IDLA is a state-funded online learning program that offers virtual courses to Idaho students, including classes that let high schoolers earn college credits. The decline in those courses could limit student access to affordable college classes, particularly in rural communities where schools rely on IDLA to expand course offerings. Simmons said the declines are largely because of course fees schools and students must pay after legislators slashed about half of the virtual program’s budget and limited its scope during the 2026 legislative session. “We used to waive the course fee for a dual credit class, so we didn’t charge a fee,” Simmons told several trustees and school administrators Thursday. Previously, students could use Advanced Opportunities dollars to cover the cost of college credits when taking dual credit courses through IDLA. A new law requires IDLA to charge a fee of $40 for classes that are a graduation requirement or $100 for classes that aren’t. In a survey of rural schools, Simmons said 70% of responding districts cited the course fee as the reason students weren’t taking dual credit courses. “I don’t think this was an intentional outcome of the legislation,” Simmons said. Simmons doesn’t know where students are turning to take college courses instead. To find out, “we’re trying to do some collaborative data collection, so we can bring a full picture back to the State Board and the state Legislature,” he said. Brett Arnzen, board chair at the Highland School District in Craigmont, said his district will have to make changes if IDLA “continues on the path it does.” The district works IDLA’s fees into its longtime supplemental levy. But as the levy becomes more difficult to pass — gaining approval by just three votes last year and 150 votes this year — Arnzen worries about asking for more. The enrollment picture extends beyond college courses. Over the summer, IDLA enrolled 8,608 students – 2,200 above what it’s funded to serve. Currently, 12,056 students are enrolled for the fall semester – 806 over what the statewide online school is funded for. This year, IDLA received state funds to serve 32,000 students. The program enrolled 56,000 students last year, before the Legislature cut $13.4 million from IDLA’s $26 million budget. Across the country, Democrats flipped hundreds of state legislative seats, won control of several GOP-held chambers, broke veto-proof supermajorities and won a majority of governorships. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star) The blue wave that swept across Tuesday’s midterm election will deliver Democrats new power over state government, giving them the opportunity to advance long-sought policy changes. Democrats flipped hundreds of seats, won control of several GOP-held chambers, broke veto-proof supermajorities and won a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Democratic lawmakers from multiple states pledged to use their new statehouse power to attack rising prices, protect reproductive rights, pass new gun safety measures and grow the housing supply. The changed landscape also gives state Democratic leaders more power to oppose the agenda of President Donald Trump, said Marc Farinella, senior advisor to the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy. That may mean opposing Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts, Farinella said, or bolstering state funding of Medicaid and food stamps, both of which have faced significant federal cuts under Trump. Legislating will prove much easier in states with newly won Democratic trifectas, where the party controls both chambers and the governor’s office. Those states include Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. But newly divided governments in other states — Iowa, Ohio, Georgia, Texas — could result in gridlock. Following the midterms, state legislatures will see their biggest leadership shakeup in years, as the National Conference of State Legislatures expects nearly half of state chambers to have new leaders next session. “None of us have ever been in a majority, so it’s a big learning curve,” said Arizona state Rep. Nancy Gutierrez, assistant House minority leader. She said Democrats, who will control Phoenix for the first time in 60 years, are connecting with their counterparts from other states, such as Colorado, that have swung from red to blue. The Pennsylvania state Senate flipped to Democratic control for the first time since 1978, handing the party a resounding trifecta after Gov. Josh Shapiro sailed to reelection. Already, Shapiro and Democratic state lawmakers have pledged to revive a slew of policies that had previously passed the state House but died in the Republican-controlled Senate. Those include raising the state’s minimum wage to $15 an hour, codifying abortion rights, passing a law to allow survivors of sexual abuse to sue their abusers and increasing funding for mass transit. “I think here in Pennsylvania we made very, very clear at the state level and the federal level that we are rejecting Donald Trump’s policies and we want to see costs come down,” Shapiro said Wednesday. “And now you’ve got an opportunity to see that happen in Harrisburg and in Washington.” At the same time, Farinella said, this week’s “historically forceful rebuke of Trump and his agenda” will prompt an as yet undetermined response from Republicans. items.body: The chair of the Idaho Democratic Party credits Tuesday’s sweep of three swing districts in the Legislature to listening to voters over the past year and focusing on solutions to challenges they are facing. Democrats picked up one seat in the Senate and five in the House. The party will now hold 21 seats in the Idaho Legislature in January, but Republicans still carry a supermajority with 84 seats. C hair Lauren Necochea said the six flipped seats will put Democrats in a better position to make good policy and stop bad bills that harm Idahoans. “What we heard from people is that affordability, healthcare — those regular kitchen table economic concerns — are what are on the top of people’s minds,” Necochea told EdNews in a Wednesday afternoon phone call. She said Democrats have solutions in that regard, while Republicans just shrug and hope the free market will take care of it. Over the next two months before the 2027 session begins, she said the Democratic caucus will work to formalize an agenda based on what the candidates ran on. Democrats want to remove the state’s grocery tax, bring back the child tax credit, which expired in January , and restore cuts to Medicaid. Necochea said the party also wants to end “sweetheart deals” with data centers and to stop giving tax breaks to wealthy individuals and profitable corporations. House Bill 93, which created the tax credit in 2025, passed 42-28 in the House and 20-15 in the Senate. “We’re spending $50 million a year on vouchers while we’re cutting Medicaid so deeply that moms are getting letters that their child with a disability is going to have their therapies limited,” Necochea said. Democrats currently hold three of 20 seats on the powerful Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. Necochea said the national landscape motivated swing district voters because they saw just how far Republicans would go to rubber-stamp the Trump administration, which she said has devastated farmers and made everything more expensive. “We don’t have a single Republican leader in Idaho who has spoken out against any of these really harmful actions,” she said. When asked if there is a particular seat Necochea is most proud that Democrats won on Tuesday, she said she is “proud of all of our candidates.”

(Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Idaho Capital Sun) In Idaho’s general election on Tuesday, some voters were voting hours after polls had closed in the state’s second most populated county. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican, attends a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Voting bled into Wednesday. The last voter in Canyon County cast their ballot at 12:20 a.m., Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane said in an interview Wednesday morning. In Idaho, polls close at 8 p.m. local time. But voters can still cast votes if they are in line by the deadline. And in Canyon County in southwest Idaho, some voters waited in lines for more than four hours, McGrane said. The lines there, driven by high turnout and long ballots, were one of his biggest challenges of the night. “The interesting thing, both visiting with the poll workers and watching some of the news outlets that visited out there, the voters were really patient, really kind, very determined to want to be able to cast their vote. I think it was incredible just to see the sense of community out there,” McGrane said. “Regardless, I think we owe it to the voters, and we’ve certainly heard some feedback just in terms of how frustrating that was. We want to make sure the voting process goes smoothly.” The lines were a sign of a bigger trend. In Tuesday’s general election for statewide offices, congressional seats, legislative seats and ballot measures, including an abortion ballot initiative, Idaho voters turned out at high rates. A midterm record high of 731,980 voters cast ballots, based on initial voter turnout data from the Secretary of State’s Office. Overall, it seems likely that registered voters turned out in the high 60% range to vote in the election, McGrane said. Besides the long lines in Canyon County, the day was fairly smooth, he said. Nearly 99% of voters cast ballots in that race — more than any statewide ballot measure. Voters rejected it, with nearly 56% voting no, according to unofficial election results . “I do think the fact that more ballots were cast on Prop 1 than any of the other statewide races indicate that it was driving some people to the polls, particularly to vote on that issue,” Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler said in an interview. The drive to turn out was likely twofold, she said: Voters tend to care deeply about abortion and reproductive healthcare issues, and there was active campaigning from both sides. But the blue wave in midterms across the country — where Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, and won control of some state legislatures and most governorships — didn’t extend to Idaho. Republican incumbents in all statewide offices and the state’s congressional delegation all easily secured reelection. Kettler wasn’t surprised. “Idaho is a solidly Republican state. Voters soundly defeated a measure that would have restored access to abortion in the state, a sharp contrast with outcomes in three other states that expanded or enshrined abortion rights. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Nationwide results for abortion ballot initiatives on Tuesday night largely favored protecting access to abortion and other reproductive care, with the exception of Idaho, where a measure that would have restored access to abortion was soundly defeated. Idaho’s outcome stood in stark contrast to the other three ballot questions, with 56% voting against the approval of Proposition 1 and 44% voting in favor, nearly the inverse of Missouri’s outcome, where 55% of voters struck down an amendment that would have reinstated the ban that was overturned through a ballot initiative in 2024. O ther abortion-related measures were on the ballot in Nevada and Virginia, two states where abortion is already accessible until 24 weeks and 26 weeks of pregnancy, respectively. Voters in both of those states passed constitutional amendments ensuring the right to abortion. The outcome in Idaho ensures the state’s abortion ban remains intact. The ban prohibits abortion at any stage of pregnancy with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. Blaine Conzatti, president of the Idaho Family Policy Center, the organization that helped craft the ban and campaigned against the initiative, said in a statement that “abortion advocates fundamentally misunderstood Idaho.” “As we proved last night, a broad majority of Idaho voters support our pro-life laws,” Conzatti said. “This is what happens when Christians speak out and get engaged — we win.” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families and lead organizer of the initiative, said in a statement that more than $1.3 million in donations from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and the Catholic Diocese of Boise fueled a disinformation campaign about what the law would do. “We’re encouraging Idahoans to reach out to their lawmakers, particularly those politicians who encouraged voters to reject Prop 1 and wait for a legislative fix, and demand needed exceptions in the coming session,” Folwell said. A federal appeals court ruled on Oct. 30 that Idaho’s law does not include exceptions for a pregnant person whose physical or mental health is in jeopardy by continuing the pregnancy, a situation that Idaho doctors have repeatedly said puts them in a position to feel compelled to wait until a patient’s life is in danger before acting. A peer-reviewed study published in 2025 in JAMA showed 114 OB-GYNs left Idaho or stopped practicing obstetrics between August 2022 and December 2024, the first two years after the ban took effect. That number represents 43% of the 268 physicians practicing obstetrics statewide. Several of those who left have said publicly that the ban made it more difficult to do their jobs without fear of criminal prosecution. Providers found guilty of violating the ban face up to five years in prison, the revocation of their medical license and up to $20,000 in civil penalties. Many doctors who have continued to practice obstetrics and gynecology in Idaho say the loss of those providers has increased their workload to a stressful and at times dangerous degree. In the months leading up to the vote, Idaho women shared their stories of needing to seek care in other states, including Utah , because of fatal fetal anomalies, along with others who said their care during a miscarriage was delayed, causing dangerous infections. With the failure of the ballot measure, pregnant patients who need an abortion will continue to need to seek care in other states. items.body: The Idaho Legislature unanimously approved placing the non-binding poll of state guns on the ballot through House Bill 932 this year. (Yves Adams/Getty Images) In a non-binding vote, Idaho voters nominated a lever-action rifle, dubbed the “Gun that Won the West” to be the state’s official gun. The gun, the Winchester Model 1873, had the backing from about 31% of Idaho voters, the highest share of any of the guns on the ballot in Tuesday’s general election, according to unofficial results from the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office at 12:30 p.m. Wednesday. All of Idaho’s 44 counties were reporting election results by then. A digital representation of a Winchester 1873. (Photo courtesy of Robert Logan/Idaho Secretary of State’s Office) The vote tees up a decision by the Idaho Legislature to potentially join 10 other states that have official state guns. Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. None of the six guns — placed on the ballot in a unanimous vote by the Legislature — received a majority vote. Here’s how all the guns on the list fared with voters this year: Winchester Model 1873 “Gun that Won the West” (.44-40): 31.1% of the vote, or 164,394 votes. Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30): 25.32% of the vote, or 133,859 votes. 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver, or “Peacemaker,” (.45 Colt): 15.26% of the vote, or 80,699 votes. Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06): 12.45% of the vote, or 65,818 votes. Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol (.45 ACP): 8.78% of the vote, or 46,405 votes. M1 Garand rifle (.30-06): 7.09% of the vote, or 37,500 votes. None of the guns on Idaho’s ballot have developmental ties to the state, unlike the official guns in some other states, like Utah . If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. House Majority Leader Jason Monks, R-Meridian, said in an interview last month that he pushed to put the question on the ballot to help drum up voter turnout. The measure, called an advisory question, had the lowest share of ballots cast of any of the statewide ballot measures. About 70% of voters cast votes in the race for the state gun, out of the more than 731,000 of voters who turned out to the polls for this election, unofficial election results show. Nearly 99% of voters cast votes on Proposition 1, a ballot initiative — which voters rejected — that sought to repeal Idaho’s near-total abortion ban. About 97% of Idaho voters cast ballots on each of the constitutional amendments: A successful one to declare English as the state’s official language , and a failed one that would’ve revoked voters’ powers to legalize marijuana and other drugs . Idaho voters turned out to vote at high rates this year in a midterm election, when voters tend to vote less. About 69% of the state’s registered voters cast ballots, early data show. Tuesday was still a very good night for Idaho Republicans. The GOP again swept every statewide race — with no after-midnight vote count suspense. Idaho will again send an all-Republican delegation to Congress, as Sen. Jim Risch and Reps. Mike Simpson and Russ Fulcher dodged a wave election that flipped the House and Senate to the Democrats. Last and certainly not least, the Republicans’ all-in opposition to Proposition 1 appeared to pay dividends. Party leadership and key Republican officeholders banded together against Prop 1, and 56% of voters rejected a voter initiative seeking to overturn Idaho’s near-complete abortion ban. So, a predictably red election night in Idaho? Generally yes, but not exactly typical. This will come as no comfort to Democratic loyalists who are comparing Idaho’s results with the stunning upsets in GOP fortresses such as South Carolina, Texas and Kansas (and perhaps, depending on the final tallies, Mississippi and Alaska). Nor will this comfort Proposition 1 supporters, after what became an unsurprisingly bitter campaign over reproductive rights and restrictions. Idaho progressives were mourning on Wednesday, while many Idaho conservatives were celebrating. But despite everything that went well for the Idaho GOP Tuesday — and there was a lot of that — this wasn’t another regular Republican rout. For starters, the Democrats picked up six legislative seats , one in the Senate, five in the House. On the surface, this only changes the Legislature around the margins. Republicans still hold 28 of the Senate’s 35 seats, and 56 of the 70 spots in the House. But let’s look under the surface. Six additional legislative seats should give the Democrats some additional spots on key Statehouse committees. The first place to watch: the budget-writing Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. Four years ago, House Speaker Mike Moyle assigned nine Republicans and one Democrat to JFAC, arguing that Democrats had long been overrepresented on the Legislature’s most powerful committee. By sheer math, the Democrats now have one-fifth of the House’s seats, which could again get them a second spot on the House’s side of JFAC. In a similar vein, Democrats might wind up with additional seats on the Senate State Affairs Committee and, possibly, the House Education Committee. Idaho State Sen. items.body: A "Stop Prop 1" sign leans up against the wall during an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, held at the Boise Centre in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1, the ballot initiative that sought to legalize abortion in the state up to fetal viability or in emergencies, and would have enumerated rights to other types of reproductive healthcare. The Associated Press called the race at 12:35 a.m. Wednesday. The voter-led ballot initiative received 43.68% of the vote, or 286,909 votes in the 2026 general election, as of 2:37 a.m. on Wednesday. More than 56.32% voted against it, early results showed. The proposition needed a simple majority of votes to pass. Idahoans United for Women and Families, the group formed to author and support the initiative, conceded that it did not pass in a press release sent just after 12:20 a.m. Idahoans United for Women and Families Executive Director Melanie Folwell speaks about Proposition 1 at the Oct. 17, 2026, No Kings rally at the Idaho Capitol in Boise. (Photo by Jim Max for the Idaho Capital Sun) “This is a tremendous, frankly gutting, loss, especially for the women, families, and physicians of Idaho,” Melanie Folwell, executive director of Idahoans United for Women and Families, said in a press release. “We will see more doctors leave the state as a result of this election. And, most urgently, women will continue to suffer needlessly under one of the most cruel abortion bans in the nation.” Election officials were still counting ballots early into Wednesday morning. Idaho’s election results do not become official until they are certified by the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24. The initiative would’ve repealed Idaho’s strict abortion ban, which outlaws nearly all abortions, except to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester when a police report is provided. Idaho’s ban carries felony prison sentences and licensing penalties for doctors who perform abortions outside of the exemptions, as well as possible civil lawsuits for a minimum of $20,000. Opponents of the ballot initiative argue that it is the state’s prerogative to protect fetuses’ lives, and that Idaho’s exemptions are sufficient to protect the mother’s life. The Idaho GOP, the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise strongly opposed the initiative. Opponents formed a group called Stop Prop 1 in response to the proposed initiative. “The people of Idaho have spoken,” Stop Prop 1 communications director Mary Strow said in a press release. “They saw through the smokescreen of deception and barrage of out-of-state funded ads that sought to rewrite our laws and reshape our values. Idaho is and will always be a state that values life and protects the unborn.” Idahoans United for Women and Families formed in 2024 to explore ways to restore abortion access in the state in response to the U.S. Supreme Court overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022, which triggered Idaho’s bans. Idahoans United in July turned in nearly 110,000 signatures to the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office to qualify for the 2026 general election ballot. In Idaho, to qualify for the general election, supporters must collect signatures from at least 6% of the registered voters statewide and from at least 6% of the registered voters in at least 18 of Idaho’s 35 legislative districts. To achieve the 6% statewide total, supporters needed 70,725 verified signatures. Its supporters argued Idaho’s laws were overreaching and potentially dangerous for pregnant women, and led to the state losing OB-GYNs. The petition to get the initiative on the ballot included signatures from Idaho voters across party lines . Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little was reelected in Tuesday’s general election and will serve a third term as the Gem State’s governor, according to the Associated Press. All other Republican candidates for statewide office were also reelected. The Associated Press called the race for Little at 10:36 p.m. Tuesday. Little addressed his supporters and several Republican officials at a downtown Boise convention hall at about 10:20 p.m. Mountain time Tuesday night, shortly before the race was officially called. “I’m humbled to have your support, grateful for your confidence, and proud to have the opportunity to continue to serve this great state,” Little told supporters Tuesday night. “Tonight’s decision results send a clear message: Idahoans want to keep moving forward. They believe in the direction the state is headed. They believe in Idaho values, and they rightfully expect us to keep delivering.” Little, a Republican from Emmett, was projected to beat his two closest challengers, Democrat Terri Pickens and independent John Stegner. As of 2:06 a.m. Mountain time Wednesday, Little had received 369,360 votes, or 57.3%, while Pickens was in second place with 206,218 votes, or 32%. Stegner was in third place, with 49,279 votes, or 7.6%. Several other candidates ran for governor as well. Libertarian Paul Sand received 10,377 votes, or 1.6%. A Constitution Party candidate who changed his name from Marvin Richardson to Pro-Life received 8,649 votes, or 1.3%. And an independent named Jacob Burnett ran as a write-in candidate and had received 227 votes. Little will serve his third, four-year term as Idaho’s governor. He was first elected governor in 2018, having previously served as lieutenant governor and a member of the Idaho Senate. In addition to Little, each of Idaho’s statewide incumbent Republican officials was also leading their re-election bids Tuesday night, according to partial unofficial election results released Tuesday by the state. The Associated Press also called the race for Idaho secretary of state in favor of Republican Secretary of State Phil McGrane at 10:31 p.m. Wednesday. Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke, Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador, Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf, Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth and Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield won their re-election bids as well. Idaho Lt. Gov. Scott Bedke leads Democrat Eric Myricks Idaho’s lieutenant governor serves as president of the Idaho Senate but only votes in cases of a tie vote. The lieutenant governor also serves as acting governor while the governor is out of the state or unable to perform the duties of office. (Photo courtesy of the Special Collections and Archives, Albertsons Library, Boise State University) Idahoans are encouraged to participate in a two-day event this week that honors the environmental and political legacy of Cecil Andrus, Idaho’s longest-serving governor. Share your ‘Cece story’: Boise State’s Andrus Center will host ‘History Harvest’ for book project The Andrus for Idaho: History Harvest event, hosted by the Boise State University Andrus Center, includes several panel discussions and presentations from some of the people who knew Andrus best, as well as an “Antiques Roadshow”-style History Harvest, which encourages Idahoans to bring in photos, memorabilia, artifacts, letters and oral histories from Andrus’ time in office to have them documented and archived. The two-day event will begin at 9 a.m. Friday and 9:45 a.m. Saturday at SPACE in Boise State University’s Albertsons Library, 1865 Friendship Lane on BSU’s campus. Both days of the event will go through the afternoon, and the public can join the activities at anytime throughout the day. The Andrus Center is also looking for volunteers to help with the event, including set-up beforehand, guiding visitors and helping at informational stations during the event and tear down and archival work afterward. To register as a volunteer, fill out this Google form online . Who was Cecil Andrus? Cecil Andrus, the last Democrat to serve as Idaho’s governor, died at age 85 in 2017. He was the only person to serve four terms – a nonconsecutive 14 years – as Idaho governor. But his service to the state and nation extended far beyond that one role. After serving in the U.S. Navy during the Korean War, he was concerned about the direction of Idaho’s public schools and ran for the state Senate in 1960 at just 28 years old, winning the seat. That began a longtime tenure in state politics, with his first stint as Idaho governor from 1971-1977. Serving as governor would eventually help prepare him for his role as U.S. secretary of the Interior in the Jimmy Carter administration from 1977-1981. He again was elected Idaho governor from 1987-1995. As Idaho’s population changes and grows, Emily Wakild, the Cecil D. Andrus endowed chairwoman for environment and public lands in the School of the Environment, College of Arts and Sciences, said the event is a way to bring the state’s history to life — and to capture the memories and items related to Andrus’ political life before it’s too late. Volunteers will be on-hand to scan photos, letters and other documents, while others will be available to record oral histories and personal stories about Andrus. Submissions large and small are welcome from Idahoans from all walks of life, Wakild said. “Within our history circles there’s this recognition that there are silences in archives,” Wakild said in an interview. “And there’s ways that we can account for them, but one of the best is to do a community archiving event and just simply ask people what they want to have remembered. That itself articulates, I think, some of the really strong values of the Andrus Center, which are public dialog, public interaction with lots of different perspectives and public ideas about moving forward.” Many of the people who worked with Andrus are aging, and organizers of the event hope to capture a more contextual picture of Andrus and his politics before they pass on, Wakild said. “We especially want to get people that do have those memories,” Wakild said. “But we also want people that have been here 10 minutes — people that can say, ‘oh, I moved here.
